items.title: CQC State of Care: more than 80,000 children wait over a year for community health care
items.source: Healthcare Management UK (reporting the CQC State of Care report)
items.summary: The Care Quality Commission's annual State of Care report found that more than 80,000 children and young people in England had waited over a year for community health appointments. Children were far more likely than adults to face year-long waits, with many waiting for autism and ADHD assessments.
items.why: Community services include speech and language therapy, so long waits can mean children who communicate without speech go without specialist input for a large part of their early years.

items.title: Early years results show a wide gap for children with SEND
items.summary: The Department for Education's 2025-26 Early Years Foundation Stage Profile results showed 72.3% of Reception pupils reached a good level of development, a record high. Among pupils with SEND the figure was 24.1%, compared with 80.5% for pupils without SEND.
items.why: Communication and language is one of the prime areas measured at age five, so the gap shows how early pre-verbal and non-verbal children fall behind the expected milestones.

items.title: Where the SEND reforms stand after the consultation
items.summary: The government has still not published its response to the SEND consultation that closed in May, though the Department for Education says it remains committed to the timetable set out in the February Schools White Paper. Lucy Powell is now Education Secretary, Georgia Gould still leads on SEND, and Individual Support Plans are planned from 2029 with no changes to EHCPs before at least September 2030.
items.why: Families and schools still do not know the final shape of plans and legal protections, so current EHCP rights and processes continue to apply for now.

items.title: Bradford opens its first centre to help children with complex SEND stay in school
items.summary: Bradford Council has opened the SCIL Centre at Margaret McMillan Primary School to support children with complex special educational needs from across the district. The council says it has already helped reduce permanent exclusions and will act as a training hub for school staff.
items.why: Bradford families of children with complex communication needs may see more specialist advice reach mainstream classrooms rather than relying on a move to another setting.

items.title: DfE surveys point to gaps in specialist support in mainstream schools
items.summary: Special Needs Jungle brought together recent Department for Education survey findings showing that a fifth of parents whose child with SEND needed speech and language therapy said it was not received. School leaders also reported shortages of teaching assistants, and many cited funding and local availability as barriers to using speech and language support staff.
items.why: The figures suggest therapy and in-class support for children who communicate without speech is still patchy, which matters as the reforms ask mainstream schools to do more.

items.title: First DfE SEND training for teachers includes a speech, language and communication module
items.summary: The first set of Department for Education SEND and inclusion training materials for schools, developed by Ambition Institute, covers inclusive teaching and a closer look at speech, language and communication development. Speech and Language UK welcomed the focus but criticised the absence of developmental language disorder and the lack of practical classroom strategies.
items.why: Teachers will be expected to understand communication development, which could shape how classrooms respond to pupils who are pre-verbal and non-verbal.

items.title: Petition to keep SEND legal rights passes 100,000 signatures
items.summary: A parliamentary petition calling on the government to keep existing SEND legal rights passed 100,000 signatures on 30 September, the level at which Parliament considers a debate. The petition was started by a 15-year-old autistic campaigner and is supported by the Save Our Children's Rights coalition.
items.why: The scale of the response shows how concerned many families are about future entitlements, and a debate could put questions about EHCP protections on the parliamentary record.

items.title: RCSLT Bulletin focuses on AAC for its autumn issue
items.source: Royal College of Speech and Language Therapists
items.summary: The autumn issue of the RCSLT Bulletin marks AAC Awareness Month with a focus on augmentative and alternative communication services. Its cover feature looks at progress and obstacles for children who need AAC, including common myths and practical tips.
items.why: It gives therapists and families current professional thinking on AAC for children, including the misconceptions that can delay a child being offered a communication aid.

items.title: Speech and language therapists press for investment ahead of the Budget
items.source: Royal College of Speech and Language Therapists
items.summary: The RCSLT's Invest in SLT campaign is asking supporters to email the Prime Minister to make speech and language therapy a priority in the 28 October Budget. Earlier in September the college backed a Health Bill amendment that would require a strategy on access, waiting times and the workforce.
items.why: Funding and workforce decisions in the Budget will affect how quickly children who communicate without speech can be assessed and supported by a therapist.

items.title: Communication Matters holds its international AAC conference in Leeds
items.summary: The Communication Matters International AAC Conference took place at the University of Leeds from 13 to 15 September 2026, followed by an AAC study day on 16 September. The event brings together AAC users, families, therapists, educators and researchers, and this year coincided with the charity's 40th anniversary.
items.why: The UK's main AAC gathering being held in West Yorkshire gave local families and professionals direct access to current practice and research on communication aids.

items.title: SEND tribunal appeals reach a record quarterly high
items.summary: Official tribunal statistics show 8,800 SEND appeals were registered between April and June 2026, the highest quarterly figure on record and 22% more than a year earlier. The open caseload rose to 18,000, and most listed SEND hearings in 2025-26 were postponed.
items.why: Families who disagree with a council decision on an EHCP face longer waits for a hearing, which can delay agreed provision such as therapy or communication support.

items.title: Councils warn of recruitment risks to the Experts at Hand plan
items.summary: Draft SEND reform plans submitted by councils to the Department for Education flag difficulty recruiting speech and language therapists, educational psychologists and occupational therapists for the 1.8 billion pound Experts at Hand scheme. Some councils also raised concerns about one-year funding and a possible rise in EHCP requests during the transition.
items.why: If therapist posts cannot be filled, the promised local bank of specialists may reach schools slowly, affecting children who rely on therapy to develop their communication.

items.title: Solihull area SEND inspection published
items.summary: Ofsted and the CQC graded the Solihull local area partnership in the middle of their three-point scale after an inspection in July 2026. Inspectors praised multi-agency working and support for speech and language needs, but said the quality of EHC plans, preparation for adulthood and health assessment waits needed to improve.
items.why: Area inspections are now looking at speech and language support as part of judging local SEND services, which gives families a public measure of how well their area is doing.

items.title: Wakefield approves 10 million pound special school scheme
items.summary: Wakefield Council's cabinet approved a 10 million pound plan to turn a former regional fire control centre into a school with up to 120 specialist places for pupils with social, emotional and mental health needs. The project uses Department for Education high needs capital funding and aims to let more children be educated closer to home.
items.why: More local specialist places could ease pressure across Wakefield's SEND system, including for children whose distress is linked to difficulty being understood.

items.title: DfE consults on upfront SEND funding for mainstream schools and on EOTAS
items.summary: The Department for Education opened a consultation on letting councils pass more SEND funding directly to mainstream schools through a local SEND inclusion formula, starting with the 2027 to 2028 financial year. A separate consultation on education otherwise than at school opened the same day, and both closed on 18 September 2026.
items.why: How money reaches schools will influence whether they can fund communication aids, training and therapy time without waiting for an EHCP.

items.title: EHCP numbers rise to almost 719,000
items.summary: Official figures show 718,838 education, health and care plans were in place in England in January 2026, up 12.5% on the previous year, and 110,708 new plans were started during 2025. Only 46.1% of new plans were issued within the 20-week legal time limit.
items.why: With more than half of new plans arriving late, many families of children with complex communication needs wait well beyond the legal timescale for agreed support.
